focus: Seven previously unreviewed known-wrong examples on already-loaded, mock-eligible original AQA AS Maths functions flashcards, particularly composite/inverse mapping and f(x) inverse graph reflections.
effect: No new flashcards, no new Maths Year 2 mock content, original core fronts/backs/accept alternatives/saved IDs unchanged. Add 1 correct and 2 wrong examples per original ID with strict guard and real marking regression.
limits: Even explicit known-wrong probes do not certify every unseen response.
Full Year 1 Pure Maths specification completeness remains separately under audit.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: When does a function have an inverse over its domain?
accept: A function has an inverse on its domain when it is injective, so no two different inputs have the same output.
reject: Every many-to-one function has an inverse on its unchanged domain.
A function with two different inputs mapping to one output is always invertible.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What must hold for the composite function f(g(x)) to be defined?
rows.originalBack: The output of g must lie in the domain of f.
accept: For f after g, all outputs of g being used must be acceptable inputs to f.
reject: Only g needs to be defined: f need never accept the values that g produces.
For f(g(x)), the result of g must always be outside the domain of f.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What geometric transformation maps y=f(x) to y=f⁻¹(x)?
accept: The graph of the inverse function is obtained by reflecting the original in y = x.
reject: Reflect the graph in the x-axis to obtain f inverse.
Reflect the graph in the y-axis to obtain f inverse.

rows.subject: Maths
accept: A one-to-one mapping assigns different output values to any two different input values.
reject: Two distinct inputs may have the same output and the function will still be one-to-one.
A one-to-one function must send every input to the same single output.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What must be true before a function has an inverse over its domain?
accept: The function must be injective, with no repeated output for different inputs.
reject: It must be many-to-one so two inputs can give the same output.
An inverse exists over the same domain even if the function is not one-to-one.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: How is the domain of f⁻¹ related to f?
rows.originalBack: It is the range of f.
accept: The inputs allowed for f inverse are exactly the outputs in the range of f.
reject: The domain of the inverse is made of values that the original function never outputs.
The inverse always has every real number as its domain, regardless of f's range.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: How is the range of f⁻¹ related to f?
rows.originalBack: It is the domain of f.
accept: The possible outputs of the inverse are the original function's domain values.
reject: The inverse range always consists of inputs that are outside the original function's domain.
The inverse always has all real numbers as its range, regardless of f's domain.
